# Scope

Fitted model objects in R often carry more than they need for prediction.
A `glm` object keeps the training data, the fitted values, the residuals, and the environment of its formula.
That is fine for a single model.
It adds up when `resample()`, `benchmark()`, or `tune()` keep one model per resampling iteration with `store_models = TRUE`.

The [butcher](https://cran.r-project.org/package=butcher) package from the tidymodels ecosystem removes these components while keeping the model usable for prediction.
This post shows how to apply it to a single learner and how to wrap it in a callback so that every model stored by [mlr3](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com) and [mlr3tuning](https://mlr3tuning.mlr-org.com) gets shrunk right after training.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)
library(mlr3tuning)
library(mlr3pipelines)
library(mlr3misc)
library(butcher)
```
:::


We measure the size of an object by serializing it.
This is the number of bytes the object needs on disk or when it is sent to a parallel worker.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size = function(x) {
  round(length(serialize(x, connection = NULL)) / 1024^2, digits = 2L)
}
```
:::


# Butcher a single model

We train a logistic regression on the spam task with 4601 emails and 57 features.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
task = tsk("spam")
learner = lrn("classif.log_reg", predict_type = "prob")
learner$train(task)

serialized_size(learner$model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4.44
```


:::
:::


The model needs about 4.4 MB.
The function `weigh()` lists the components of the model object sorted by size in MB.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
weigh(learner$model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 101 × 2
   object              size
   <chr>              <dbl>
 1 qr.qr             2.16  
 2 residuals         0.333 
 3 fitted.values     0.333 
 4 linear.predictors 0.333 
 5 weights           0.333 
 6 prior.weights     0.333 
 7 y                 0.333 
 8 effects           0.0773
 9 family.variance   0.0440
10 family.dev.resids 0.0440
# ℹ 91 more rows
```


:::
:::


The QR decomposition is the largest component.
The residuals, fitted values, linear predictors, weights, and the response each take another 0.33 MB.
Prediction needs only a fraction of this.

We predict on the task, butcher the model, and write it back into the learner.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
prediction = learner$predict(task)
learner$model = butcher(learner$model)

serialized_size(learner$model)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.34
```


:::
:::


The model shrank to roughly half its size.
The predictions of the butchered model are identical to the original predictions.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
all.equal(prediction, learner$predict(task))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


The function `butcher()` only removes components that the `predict()` method of the model class does not use.
It keeps the QR decomposition because `predict.glm()` needs it to compute standard errors.

::: {.callout-warning}
A butchered model has lost information.
Functions such as `summary()`, `residuals()`, or `fitted()` may fail or return wrong results on it.
Only butcher models that you need for prediction.
:::

# Resample callback

We now want to shrink every model that `resample()` stores.
Callbacks run code at specific stages of the resampling loop.
We create a resample callback with [`mlr3::callback_resample()`](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/reference/callback_resample.html).
The stage `on_resample_end` runs after the learner has been trained and has made its predictions.
The context object gives access to the learner of the current iteration.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
callback = callback_resample("butcher",
  on_resample_end = function(callback, context) {
    context$learner$model = butcher::butcher(context$learner$model)
  }
)
```
:::


We call `butcher()` with the package prefix because the callback may run on a parallel worker on which `butcher` is not attached.

We run a 5-fold cross-validation twice on the same splits, once without and once with the callback.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
resampling = rsmp("cv", folds = 5L)
resampling$instantiate(task)

rr = resample(task, learner, resampling, store_models = TRUE)
rr_butchered = resample(task, learner, resampling, store_models = TRUE, callbacks = callback)
```
:::


We compare the size of the stored models.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(map(rr$learners, "model"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 19.19
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(map(rr_butchered$learners, "model"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 10.4
```


:::
:::


The five butchered models need about 9 MB less.
The callback only touches the stored models, so the performance estimate does not change.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rr$aggregate(msr("classif.auc"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
classif.auc 
   0.971403 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rr_butchered$aggregate(msr("classif.auc"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
classif.auc 
   0.971403 
```


:::
:::


The stored learners still predict new data.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rr_butchered$learners[[1L]]$predict(task)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

── <PredictionClassif> for 4601 observations: ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 row_ids   truth response  prob.spam prob.nonspam
       1    spam     spam 0.62852865 3.714714e-01
       2    spam     spam 0.99139839 8.601607e-03
       3    spam     spam 0.99999999 5.408266e-09
     ---     ---      ---        ---          ---
    4599 nonspam  nonspam 0.03097766 9.690223e-01
    4600 nonspam  nonspam 0.07923412 9.207659e-01
    4601 nonspam  nonspam 0.02782719 9.721728e-01
```


:::
:::


# Benchmark

`benchmark()` accepts the same callbacks.
We compare four learners with a 3-fold cross-validation.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
learners = list(
  lrn("classif.log_reg", predict_type = "prob"),
  lrn("classif.rpart", predict_type = "prob"),
  lrn("classif.nnet", predict_type = "prob", size = 5L, trace = FALSE),
  lrn("classif.ranger", predict_type = "prob", num.trees = 100L)
)

design = benchmark_grid(task, learners, rsmp("cv", folds = 3L))

bmr = benchmark(design, store_models = TRUE)
bmr_butchered = benchmark(design, store_models = TRUE, callbacks = callback)
```
:::


We compute the size of the stored models for each learner.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
models_size = function(bmr) {
  map_dbl(bmr$resample_results$resample_result, function(rr) serialized_size(map(rr$learners, "model")))
}

data.table(
  learner_id = map_chr(bmr$resample_results$resample_result, function(rr) rr$learner$id),
  original = models_size(bmr),
  butchered = models_size(bmr_butchered)
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        learner_id original butchered
            <char>    <num>     <num>
1: classif.log_reg     8.96      4.76
2:   classif.rpart     0.17      0.12
3:    classif.nnet     0.29      0.18
4:  classif.ranger     4.98      4.75
```


:::
:::


How much `butcher()` saves depends on the model class.
The logistic regression, the decision tree, and the neural network lose 30 to 50 percent of their size.
The random forest barely changes because its size comes from the trees, which it needs for prediction.
For model classes without a `butcher` method, `butcher()` returns the model unchanged.
You can check which classes are supported in the [butcher documentation](https://butcher.tidymodels.org/articles/available-axe-methods.html).

# Tuning

Tuning with `store_models = TRUE` stores one model per resampling iteration and hyperparameter configuration.
Tuning instances take tuning callbacks, which can include the resample stages.
We create one with [`mlr3tuning::callback_batch_tuning()`](https://mlr3tuning.mlr-org.com/reference/callback_batch_tuning.html).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
callback_tuning = callback_batch_tuning("butcher",
  on_resample_end = function(callback, context) {
    context$learner$model = butcher::butcher(context$learner$model)
  }
)
```
:::


We tune the complexity parameter of a decision tree with 20 random configurations and a 3-fold cross-validation.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
learner_rpart = lrn("classif.rpart", cp = to_tune(1e-4, 1e-1, logscale = TRUE))

instance = tune(
  tuner = tnr("random_search"),
  task = task,
  learner = learner_rpart,
  resampling = rsmp("cv", folds = 3L),
  term_evals = 20L,
  store_models = TRUE,
  callbacks = callback_tuning
)
```
:::


The archive contains a benchmark result with the 60 butchered models.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
models = map(instance$archive$benchmark_result$resample_results$resample_result, function(rr) {
  map(rr$learners, "model")
})

serialized_size(models)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.82
```


:::
:::


# Graph learners

The model of a `GraphLearner` is a list with one state per `PipeOp`.
`butcher()` does not know this list and returns it unchanged.
We need to butcher the model in each state.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
callback_graph = callback_resample("butcher_graph",
  on_resample_end = function(callback, context) {
    model = context$learner$model
    for (id in names(model)) {
      if (!is.null(model[[id]]$model)) {
        model[[id]]$model = butcher::butcher(model[[id]]$model)
      }
    }
    context$learner$model = model
  }
)
```
:::


We apply the callback to a pipeline that reduces the features to 10 principal components before fitting the logistic regression.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph_learner = as_learner(po("pca", rank. = 10L) %>>% lrn("classif.log_reg"))

rr_graph = resample(task, graph_learner, resampling, store_models = TRUE)
rr_graph_butchered = resample(task, graph_learner, resampling, store_models = TRUE, callbacks = callback_graph)

serialized_size(map(rr_graph$learners, "model"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 6.05
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
serialized_size(map(rr_graph_butchered$learners, "model"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.86
```


:::
:::


The stored pipelines shrink by about a third.
The model of the PCA step has no `butcher` method and stays as it is.

# Conclusion

The `butcher` package removes data, calls, and environments that a model does not need for prediction.
Wrapped in a callback, it shrinks every model that `resample()`, `benchmark()`, or `tune()` stores.
This keeps large benchmark results in memory and makes them faster to save and to transfer from parallel workers.
Check the savings for your model class first.
For a random forest, there is little to gain.
